prompt:
A worker pulls a crate of mass 25 kg a distance of 12 m up a rough ramp inclined at 20 degrees to the horizontal. The worker applies a constant pulling force F = 160 N acting parallel to the surface of the ramp. A constant frictional force of 45 N opposes the motion. (Take g = 9.81 m s^-2).
[FIGURE PLACEHOLDER: Diagram of a crate of mass 25 kg on an inclined plane of slope angle 20 degrees. Pulling force F = 160 N is directed up the plane. Friction f = 45 N acts down the plane. Displacement along the ramp is s = 12 m.]
(a) Calculate the work done on the crate by the pulling force F. [2]
(b) Calculate the work done against friction during the 12 m displacement. [1]
(c) (i) Calculate the vertical height gained by the crate. [1]
(ii) Calculate the work done against gravity. [1]
(d) Using the principle of conservation of energy, determine the net work available to increase the kinetic energy of the crate. [1]

parts.description: Calculate work done by the applied pulling force
Calculate net work transferred to kinetic energy

part_enrichment.guidance: Award M1 for W = Fs = 160 * 12, A1 for 1920 J.
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Incorrectly multiplying by cos(20 degrees) when force is already parallel to the ramp.
Confusing work done against friction (+540 J) with work done by friction (-540 J).

part_enrichment.guidance: Award A1 for h = 12 * sin(20 degrees) = 4.10 m (accept 4.1 m).
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Using cos(20 degrees) instead of sin(20 degrees) for vertical height.

part_enrichment.guidance: Award A1 for W = mgh = 25 * 9.81 * 4.104 = 1010 J (accept 1006 J or 1000 J).
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Using full slope distance instead of vertical height.

part_enrichment.guidance: Award A1 for subtraction: 1920 - 540 - 1007 = 373 J (accept 370 J to 374 J).
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Adding wasted work to input work instead of subtracting.

mark_scheme.criterion: (c)(i) 4.1 m or 4.10 m (h = 12 * sin(20 degrees) = 4.104 m)

hints: In (a), force acts parallel to the incline, so theta = 0 degrees along the direction of displacement.
In (c)(i), vertical height h is the opposite side of the right triangle: h = s sin(theta).
In (d), subtract work done against friction and work done against gravity from the total work supplied.
solution:
(a) Because the pulling force acts parallel to the displacement along the ramp, W_pull = F * s = 160 N * 12 m = 1920 J.
(b) Work done against friction = f * s = 45 N * 12 m = 540 J.
(c)(i) Vertical height gained h = s sin(20 degrees) = 12 m * 0.34202 = 4.104 m approx 4.1 m.
(c)(ii) Work done against gravity = mgh = 25 kg * 9.81 m s^-2 * 4.104 m = 1006.5 J approx 1010 J (1.0 kJ).
(d) By conservation of energy, Net work available for kinetic energy = Total work done by pulling force - Work against friction - Work against gravity = 1920 J - 540 J - 1006.5 J = 373.5 J approx 370 J (or 374 J).
teacher_walkthrough: This question tests energy accounting on an inclined plane.
Crucial distinction: pulling force is already parallel to the ramp, so do NOT multiply by cos(20 degrees) in part (a).
Part (d) directly reinforces learning outcome 9702_t05_m01_o02 on applying energy conservation.

provenance.abstract_pattern: inclined plane work-energy audit and dissipation breakdown
provenance.independence_statement: Authored as an original multipart question auditing work against friction, gravity, and net mechanical energy transfer.
